prompt: Money is best defined as

options.label: A
options.text: any asset included in the monetary base.

options.label: B
options.text: any financial asset that earns a positive rate of return.

options.label: C
options.text: any asset that can be held as a store of value.

options.label: D
options.text: any asset that is accepted as a means of payment.

options.label: E
options.text: currency issued only by a national government.

explanation: Money is defined by its acceptability as a means of payment. An asset can have value or earn a return without serving as money if it is not generally accepted in payment.

prompt: Which of the following best illustrates an asset functioning as money?

options.label: A
options.text: An investor holds a bond to receive interest payments.

options.label: B
options.text: A household owns stock that it plans to sell in ten years.

options.label: C
options.text: A collector owns a rare coin that stores value but is not accepted at stores.

options.label: D
options.text: A customer uses a checking-account balance to pay a grocery bill.

options.label: E
options.text: A bank keeps currency in its vault as part of its reserves.

explanation: The checking-account balance is accepted directly as payment, so it is functioning as money. Merely holding a valuable financial asset does not make that asset a means of payment.

prompt: Money serves as a medium of exchange when it is used to

options.label: A
options.text: transfer purchasing power from the present to the future.

options.label: B
options.text: distinguish M1 from M2.

options.label: C
options.text: purchase goods and services without requiring direct barter.

options.label: D
options.text: express the prices of goods in a common unit.

options.label: E
options.text: measure the size of the monetary base.

explanation: As a medium of exchange, money is accepted in payment for goods and services. This function allows buyers and sellers to transact without directly exchanging one good for another.

prompt: Money serves as a unit of account when it is used to

options.label: A
options.text: state and compare the prices of different goods and services.

options.label: B
options.text: hold purchasing power for future use.

options.label: C
options.text: separate checkable deposits from savings deposits.

options.label: D
options.text: calculate currency in circulation plus bank reserves.

options.label: E
options.text: make immediate payments for purchases.

explanation: A unit of account provides a common standard in which prices and values are quoted; This makes the values of different goods and services directly comparable.

prompt: Money serves as a store of value when it is used to

options.label: A
options.text: carry purchasing power from the present into the future.

options.label: B
options.text: determine the amount of bank reserves in the monetary base.

options.label: C
options.text: quote the price of one good relative to another.

options.label: D
options.text: measure only the currency component of M1.

options.label: E
options.text: complete a transaction at the time of purchase.

explanation: A store of value allows purchasing power to be saved for later use. The function concerns holding value over time rather than making a current payment or quoting a price.

prompt: A restaurant lists a sandwich at $12 and a salad at $9. This most directly illustrates money serving as a

options.label: A
options.text: medium of exchange.

options.label: B
options.text: store of value.

options.label: C
options.text: monetary aggregate.

options.label: D
options.text: unit of account.

options.label: E
options.text: bank reserve.

explanation: The dollar prices provide a common unit for expressing and comparing the values of the two items; No payment or saving over time is required for this example.

prompt: A shopper pays $40 for a jacket using funds in a checking account. This most directly illustrates money serving as a

options.label: A
options.text: unit of account.

options.label: B
options.text: medium of exchange.

options.label: C
options.text: measure of M2 only.

options.label: D
options.text: component of bank reserves.

options.label: E
options.text: store of value.

explanation: Money is functioning as a medium of exchange because it is being transferred to complete a purchase; The transaction uses money as the accepted means of payment.

prompt: A household keeps $300 in currency for purchases it expects to make next month. This most directly illustrates money serving as a

options.label: A
options.text: checkable deposit.

options.label: B
options.text: medium of exchange.

options.label: C
options.text: unit of account.

options.label: D
options.text: measure of the monetary base only.

options.label: E
options.text: store of value.

explanation: The household is preserving purchasing power for use at a later date, so money is serving as a store of value. The funds are not yet being exchanged for a good or used to quote a price.

prompt: Which of the following is the best example of money serving as a unit of account?

options.label: A
options.text: A bank adds currency to its reserves.

options.label: B
options.text: A store posts the prices of all products in dollars.

options.label: C
options.text: A household transfers funds from savings to checking.

options.label: D
options.text: A worker keeps part of a paycheck for next month.

options.label: E
options.text: A buyer uses currency to purchase a product.

explanation: Posting prices in dollars uses money as the common measuring unit for value; The other core functions involve completing exchanges or preserving purchasing power.

prompt: Which of the following is the best example of money serving as a store of value?

options.label: A
options.text: A bank counts vault cash as part of its reserves.

options.label: B
options.text: A customer uses a debit card to pay for lunch.

options.label: C
options.text: A worker saves part of this month's earnings to spend later.

options.label: D
options.text: A business lists wages and prices in dollars.

options.label: E
options.text: A government reports M1 and M2 for the economy.

explanation: Saving earnings for later use transfers purchasing power through time; That is the store-of-value function of money.

prompt: M1 and M2 are best described as

options.label: A
options.text: the three functions that money performs.

options.label: B
options.text: two categories of bank reserves.

options.label: C
options.text: monetary aggregates used to measure the money supply.

options.label: D
options.text: measures of the price of borrowed money.

options.label: E
options.text: different measures of the monetary base only.

explanation: M1 and M2 are monetary aggregates used to quantify the money supply. They differ in the types of monetary assets included, with M2 being the broader measure under the convention used here.

prompt: Under the measurement convention used in this bank, which monetary aggregate is the narrower measure of the money supply?

options.label: A
options.text: M1

options.label: B
options.text: Bank reserves

options.label: C
options.text: MB

options.label: D
options.text: M0 plus M2

options.label: E
options.text: M2

explanation: M1 contains the most directly spendable components in the convention used here; M2 includes M1 plus additional less-liquid monetary assets, so M1 is the narrower aggregate.

prompt: Under the measurement convention used in this bank, M2 includes

options.label: A
options.text: only checkable deposits held by the public.

options.label: B
options.text: currency in circulation but no deposit balances.

options.label: C
options.text: all components of M1 plus additional less-liquid monetary assets.

options.label: D
options.text: the monetary base but not M1.

options.label: E
options.text: only bank reserves and currency in circulation.

explanation: M2 is a broader monetary aggregate than M1; It includes the components of M1 and adds savings-type and other near-money balances specified in the convention.

prompt: The monetary base is equal to

options.label: A
options.text: currency in circulation plus checkable deposits.

options.label: B
options.text: M2 minus checkable deposits.

options.label: C
options.text: bank reserves plus savings deposits.

options.label: D
options.text: currency in circulation plus bank reserves.

options.label: E
options.text: M1 plus savings deposits.

explanation: The monetary base, often labeled M0 or MB, consists of currency in circulation and bank reserves; It is a different measure from the M1 and M2 money-supply aggregates.

prompt: Which of the following is included in the monetary base?

options.label: A
options.text: Savings deposits only

options.label: B
options.text: Stock held by households

options.label: C
options.text: Currency in circulation

options.label: D
options.text: Retail money market mutual fund balances only

options.label: E
options.text: Small time deposits only

explanation: Currency in circulation is one of the two components of the monetary base; The other component is bank reserves.

prompt: Which of the following is included in the monetary base but is not currency in circulation?

options.label: A
options.text: Checkable deposits

options.label: B
options.text: Savings deposits

options.label: C
options.text: Small time deposits

options.label: D
options.text: Retail money market mutual fund balances

options.label: E
options.text: Bank reserves

explanation: Bank reserves are included with currency in circulation in the monetary base. Deposit balances held by the public belong to money-supply measures rather than being a separate component of the monetary base.

prompt: Under the measurement convention used in this bank, M1 consists of

options.label: A
options.text: M2 and bank reserves.

options.label: B
options.text: currency in circulation and small time deposits only.

options.label: C
options.text: checkable deposits and savings deposits only.

options.label: D
options.text: currency in circulation and checkable deposits.

options.label: E
options.text: currency in circulation and bank reserves.

explanation: For calculation questions in this bank, M1 includes currency in circulation and checkable deposits; Bank reserves instead belong to the monetary base.

prompt: Under the measurement convention used in this bank, which item is added to M1 when calculating M2?

options.label: A
options.text: Currency already in circulation

options.label: B
options.text: Savings deposits

options.label: C
options.text: Bank reserves

options.label: D
options.text: Checkable deposits already included in M1

options.label: E
options.text: Vault cash already counted as bank reserves

explanation: M2 includes M1 plus additional less-liquid monetary assets such as savings deposits. Currency and checkable deposits are already included in M1, while bank reserves belong to the monetary base.

prompt: Currency held by a commercial bank in its vault is classified as

options.label: A
options.text: a retail money market mutual fund balance.

options.label: B
options.text: bank reserves rather than currency in circulation.

options.label: C
options.text: a checkable deposit held by the public.

options.label: D
options.text: a savings deposit included only in M2.

options.label: E
options.text: currency in circulation rather than bank reserves.

explanation: Currency in a bank vault is part of the bank's reserves; Currency in circulation refers to currency held outside banks by the public.

prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes the monetary base from M1?

options.label: A
options.text: The monetary base and M1 always contain exactly the same components.

options.label: B
options.text: The monetary base includes only checkable deposits, while M1 includes only currency.

options.label: C
options.text: The monetary base includes M2, while M1 excludes currency.

options.label: D
options.text: The monetary base includes savings deposits, while M1 includes bank reserves.

options.label: E
options.text: The monetary base includes bank reserves, while M1 includes checkable deposits.

explanation: The monetary base is currency in circulation plus bank reserves, whereas M1 is currency in circulation plus checkable deposits under the convention used here. Currency is shared, but the second component differs.

prompt: Currency in circulation is $420 billion and checkable deposits are $680 billion. What is M1?

options.label: A
options.text: $1,100 billion

options.label: B
options.text: $680 billion

options.label: C
options.text: $260 billion

options.label: D
options.text: $420 billion

options.label: E
options.text: $1,520 billion

explanation: M1 equals currency in circulation plus checkable deposits; Adding $420 billion and $680 billion gives $1,100 billion.

prompt: M1 is $1,250 billion, savings deposits are $500 billion, small time deposits are $150 billion, and retail money market mutual fund balances are $100 billion. What is M2?

options.label: A
options.text: $750 billion

options.label: B
options.text: $2,250 billion

options.label: C
options.text: $1,500 billion

options.label: D
options.text: $1,750 billion

options.label: E
options.text: $2,000 billion

explanation: M2 equals M1 plus the additional near-money components specified in the convention. $1,250 + $500 + $150 + $100 = $2,000 billion.

prompt: Currency in circulation is $600 billion and bank reserves are $250 billion. What is the monetary base?

options.label: A
options.text: $250 billion

options.label: B
options.text: $1,100 billion

options.label: C
options.text: $600 billion

options.label: D
options.text: $350 billion

options.label: E
options.text: $850 billion

explanation: The monetary base equals currency in circulation plus bank reserves. $600 billion + $250 billion = $850 billion.

prompt: The monetary base is $900 billion and bank reserves are $275 billion. What is currency in circulation?

options.label: A
options.text: $625 billion

options.label: B
options.text: $1,175 billion

options.label: C
options.text: $900 billion

options.label: D
options.text: $525 billion

options.label: E
options.text: $275 billion

explanation: Currency in circulation equals the monetary base minus bank reserves. $900 billion - $275 billion = $625 billion.

prompt: Under the measurement convention used in this bank, which asset is included in M2 but not M1?

options.label: A
options.text: Currency held by the public

options.label: B
options.text: A savings deposit

options.label: C
options.text: A checking-account balance

options.label: D
options.text: Currency used to make a purchase

options.label: E
options.text: A checkable deposit

explanation: Savings deposits are part of the broader M2 aggregate but not the narrower M1 aggregate under the convention used here. Currency in circulation and checkable deposits are included in both.

prompt: Under the measurement convention used in this bank, a checkable deposit is included in

options.label: A
options.text: both M1 and M2.

options.label: B
options.text: bank reserves but not the money supply.

options.label: C
options.text: M2 but not M1.

options.label: D
options.text: M1 but not M2.

options.label: E
options.text: the monetary base but neither M1 nor M2.

explanation: M2 includes all of M1, and checkable deposits are a component of M1; A checkable deposit is therefore counted in both M1 and M2.

prompt: Currency in circulation is included in which of the following measures under the convention used in this bank?

options.label: A
options.text: M1 only

options.label: B
options.text: M1 and M2 but not the monetary base

options.label: C
options.text: M1, M2, and the monetary base

options.label: D
options.text: M2 only

options.label: E
options.text: the monetary base only

explanation: Currency in circulation is a component of M1; because M2 contains M1, it is also in M2. It is also one of the two components of the monetary base.

prompt: Bank reserves are included directly in which measure?

options.label: A
options.text: both M1 and M2

options.label: B
options.text: The monetary base

options.label: C
options.text: M2 only

options.label: D
options.text: M1 only

options.label: E
options.text: M1 and the monetary base

explanation: Bank reserves are a component of the monetary base; They are not a separate component of M1 or M2 because those aggregates measure money held by the public.

prompt: A buyer compares two laptops priced at $900 and $1,200 and then pays for one using a checking-account balance. In this example, money serves first as a

options.label: A
options.text: medium of exchange and then as a store of value.

options.label: B
options.text: unit of account and then as a medium of exchange.

options.label: C
options.text: store of value and then as a unit of account.

options.label: D
options.text: store of value and then as a medium of exchange.

options.label: E
options.text: medium of exchange and then as a unit of account.

explanation: The posted dollar prices let the buyer compare values, which is the unit-of-account function. Using the checking balance to complete the purchase then uses money as a medium of exchange.

prompt: Which statement correctly identifies all three functions of money?

options.label: A
options.text: Money serves as currency, bank reserves, and savings deposits.

options.label: B
options.text: Money serves as M1, M2, and the monetary base.

options.label: C
options.text: Money serves as a monetary base, a bank reserve, and a checkable deposit.

options.label: D
options.text: Money serves as a medium of exchange, a unit of account, and a store of value.

options.label: E
options.text: Money serves as a price level, an interest rate, and a financial return.

explanation: The three functions of money are medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value. M1, M2, and the monetary base are measurements or components rather than functions.

prompt: A household receives income on Friday, keeps part of it until Monday, and then uses those funds to buy groceries. Which two functions of money are illustrated in sequence?

options.label: A
options.text: Unit of account, then medium of exchange

options.label: B
options.text: Store of value, then medium of exchange

options.label: C
options.text: Unit of account, then store of value

options.label: D
options.text: Medium of exchange, then store of value

options.label: E
options.text: Medium of exchange, then unit of account

explanation: Holding the funds across several days preserves purchasing power, so money first serves as a store of value. Spending the funds on groceries then uses money as a medium of exchange.

prompt: A business posts wages at $22 per hour and later pays workers from its checking account. Which functions of money are illustrated?

options.label: A
options.text: Monetary base and medium of exchange

options.label: B
options.text: Unit of account and store of value only

options.label: C
options.text: Unit of account and medium of exchange

options.label: D
options.text: Medium of exchange and store of value only

options.label: E
options.text: Store of value and monetary measurement

explanation: Quoting the wage in dollars uses money as a unit of account. Transferring checking-account funds to pay workers uses money as a medium of exchange.

prompt: A household keeps $2,000 in a checking account for several weeks before using it to pay rent. Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The balance becomes part of bank reserves while held and becomes M2 only when paid.

options.label: B
options.text: The balance serves only as a store of value because a checkable deposit cannot make payments.

options.label: C
options.text: The balance serves as a medium of exchange while held and as a store of value when paid.

options.label: D
options.text: The balance serves only as a unit of account because checking deposits are not money.

options.label: E
options.text: The balance serves as a store of value while held and as a medium of exchange when paid.

explanation: The funds preserve purchasing power while they are held, which is the store-of-value function. When the household transfers them to the landlord, they function as a medium of exchange.

prompt: A market quotes all prices in dollars, but sellers refuse to accept dollars as payment. Which function would dollars clearly perform in that market?

options.label: A
options.text: All three functions necessarily

options.label: B
options.text: Unit of account only

options.label: C
options.text: Medium of exchange only

options.label: D
options.text: Medium of exchange and unit of account

options.label: E
options.text: Store of value only

explanation: Because prices are expressed in dollars, dollars provide the common unit for comparing value. Refusal to accept dollars as payment means the medium-of-exchange function is not established by the information given.

prompt: An asset is widely accepted by sellers in payment for goods and services. Which conclusion follows most directly?

options.label: A
options.text: The asset must represent bank reserves held by financial institutions.

options.label: B
options.text: The asset must be a savings deposit rather than M1.

options.label: C
options.text: The asset must earn interest in order to qualify as money.

options.label: D
options.text: The asset qualifies as money under the course definition.

options.label: E
options.text: The asset must be included only in the monetary base.

explanation: The defining condition for money is acceptance as a means of payment. The definition does not require the asset to earn interest or to belong to a particular deposit category.

prompt: Which statement about M1 and M2 must be true under the measurement convention used in this bank?

options.label: A
options.text: M1 contains bank reserves, so it must exceed the monetary base.

options.label: B
options.text: M2 excludes checkable deposits, so it can be smaller than M1.

options.label: C
options.text: M1 is always larger than M2 because it contains currency.

options.label: D
options.text: M2 is at least as large as M1 because M2 contains all of M1.

options.label: E
options.text: M1 and M2 are always equal because both measure the money supply.

explanation: M2 is constructed by adding specified less-liquid monetary assets to M1; Therefore M2 cannot be smaller than M1 under this classification.

prompt: Suppose M1 is $1,400 billion and the additional components included only in M2 total $900 billion. What is M2?

options.label: A
options.text: $2,300 billion

options.label: B
options.text: $900 billion

options.label: C
options.text: $500 billion

options.label: D
options.text: $1,400 billion

options.label: E
options.text: $3,700 billion

explanation: M2 equals M1 plus the additional M2-only components. $1,400 billion + $900 billion = $2,300 billion.

prompt: Suppose M2 is $2,750 billion and M1 is $1,900 billion. What is the total value of the components included in M2 but not M1?

options.label: A
options.text: $850 billion

options.label: B
options.text: $2,750 billion

options.label: C
options.text: $950 billion

options.label: D
options.text: $4,650 billion

options.label: E
options.text: $1,900 billion

explanation: The M2-only components equal M2 minus M1. $2,750 billion - $1,900 billion = $850 billion.

prompt: A household transfers $80 from a savings deposit to a checking account. Assume all other quantities are unchanged. What happens to M1 and M2 under the convention used in this bank?

options.label: A
options.text: Both M1 and M2 increase by $80.

options.label: B
options.text: Both M1 and M2 decrease by $80.

options.label: C
options.text: M1 decreases by $80, while M2 is unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: M1 is unchanged, while M2 increases by $80.

options.label: E
options.text: M1 increases by $80, while M2 is unchanged.

explanation: The transfer moves $80 from an M2-only component into a component of M1. Because both the original savings balance and the new checking balance are included in M2, total M2 is unchanged while M1 rises.

prompt: A household transfers $120 from a checking account to a savings deposit. Assume all other quantities are unchanged. What happens to M1 and M2?

options.label: A
options.text: Both M1 and M2 decrease by $120.

options.label: B
options.text: M1 is unchanged, while M2 decreases by $120.

options.label: C
options.text: M1 decreases by $120, while M2 is unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: M1 increases by $120, while M2 is unchanged.

options.label: E
options.text: Both M1 and M2 increase by $120.

explanation: The funds leave a component of M1 and enter a component included only in M2. The transfer therefore lowers M1 by $120 while leaving the broader M2 aggregate unchanged.

prompt: A person deposits $200 of currency that had been in circulation into a checking account, and the bank adds the same $200 of currency to its reserves. What happens immediately to M1 and the monetary base?

options.label: A
options.text: Both M1 and the monetary base increase by $200.

options.label: B
options.text: Both M1 and the monetary base are unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: Both M1 and the monetary base decrease by $200.

options.label: D
options.text: M1 decreases by $200 and the monetary base increases by $200.

options.label: E
options.text: M1 increases by $200 and the monetary base decreases by $200.

explanation: Within M1, currency in circulation falls by $200 while checkable deposits rise by $200, so M1 is unchanged. Within the monetary base, currency in circulation falls by $200 while bank reserves rise by $200, so the base is also unchanged.

prompt: A person withdraws $150 from a checking account as currency, and the bank's reserves fall by $150. What happens immediately to M1 and the monetary base?

options.label: A
options.text: Both M1 and the monetary base fall by $150.

options.label: B
options.text: M1 rises by $150 and the monetary base falls by $150.

options.label: C
options.text: Both M1 and the monetary base are unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: Both M1 and the monetary base rise by $150.

options.label: E
options.text: M1 falls by $150 and the monetary base rises by $150.

explanation: The withdrawal converts a checkable deposit into currency in circulation, leaving the two M1 components with the same total. It also converts bank reserves into currency in circulation, leaving the monetary base unchanged.

prompt: Currency in circulation is unchanged, but bank reserves increase by $90 billion. All deposit categories are unchanged. Which measure changes?

options.label: A
options.text: The monetary base increases by $90 billion, while M1 and M2 are unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: M2 increases by $90 billion, while M1 and the monetary base are unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: M1 increases by $90 billion, while M2 and the monetary base are unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: All three measures increase by $90 billion.

options.label: E
options.text: All three measures remain unchanged.

explanation: Bank reserves enter directly into the monetary base but not into M1 or M2. With public currency and deposit balances unchanged, only the monetary base rises.

prompt: Checkable deposits increase by $70 billion while all other monetary components are unchanged. What happens to M1 and M2?

options.label: A
options.text: M2 rises by $70 billion while M1 is unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: M1 rises by $70 billion while M2 is unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: Both M1 and M2 decrease by $70 billion.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither M1 nor M2 changes because checkable deposits are bank reserves.

options.label: E
options.text: Both M1 and M2 increase by $70 billion.

prompt: Savings deposits increase by $60 billion while all other monetary components are unchanged. What happens under the convention used in this bank?

options.label: A
options.text: M1 increases by $60 billion, while M2 is unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: Both M1 and M2 decrease by $60 billion.

options.label: C
options.text: The monetary base increases by $60 billion, while M1 and M2 are unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: M2 increases by $60 billion, while M1 is unchanged.

options.label: E
options.text: Both M1 and M2 increase by $60 billion.

prompt: Currency in circulation is $520 billion, checkable deposits are $880 billion, savings deposits are $460 billion, small time deposits are $140 billion, and retail money market mutual fund balances are $100 billion. What are M1 and M2?

options.label: A
options.text: M1 = $1,400 billion; M2 = $2,100 billion

options.label: B
options.text: M1 = $880 billion; M2 = $1,580 billion

options.label: C
options.text: M1 = $1,400 billion; M2 = $1,700 billion

options.text: M1 = $520 billion; M2 = $1,400 billion

prompt: Currency in circulation is $700 billion, bank reserves are $240 billion, and checkable deposits are $900 billion. What are the monetary base and M1?

options.label: A

options.text: Monetary base = $700 billion; M1 = $1,140 billion

options.label: E

options.text: M1 and M2 are unchanged, while the monetary base rises by $120 billion.

options.label: C
options.text: M1 and M2 each fall by $120 billion, while the monetary base is unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: All three measures are unchanged because currency is still physically present.

options.label: E
options.text: M1 rises by $120 billion, M2 is unchanged, and the base is unchanged.

explanation: M1 and M2 count currency only while it is in circulation, so both fall when public currency moves into bank reserves without a matching deposit increase. The monetary base is unchanged because the decrease in circulating currency is exactly offset by higher reserves.

prompt: Economy A has M1 of $1,800 billion, M2 of $2,600 billion, and a monetary base of $900 billion. Economy B has M1 of $1,650 billion, M2 of $2,750 billion, and a monetary base of $950 billion. Which statement is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Economy B has the larger M1, while Economy A has the larger M2 and base.

options.label: B
options.text: The two economies have equal M1-to-M2 relationships because the monetary bases are similar.

options.label: C
options.text: Economy A has the larger M1, M2, and monetary base.

options.label: D
options.text: Economy B has the larger M1 and M2, while Economy A has the larger base.

options.label: E
options.text: Economy A has the larger M1, while Economy B has the larger M2 and monetary base.

explanation: M1 is $150 billion larger in Economy A. M2 is $150 billion larger in Economy B, and the monetary base is $50 billion larger in Economy B.

prompt: A token is used to quote all prices in a market and is accepted for purchases, but people generally exchange it immediately rather than holding it between transactions. Which functions are directly established by the description?

options.label: A
options.text: Medium of exchange and store of value

options.label: B
options.text: All three functions necessarily

options.label: C
options.text: Store of value only

options.label: D
options.text: Unit of account and store of value

options.label: E
options.text: Unit of account and medium of exchange

explanation: Quoting prices establishes the unit-of-account function, and acceptance for purchases establishes the medium-of-exchange function. The description does not establish that people rely on the token to carry purchasing power through time.

prompt: An asset loses value rapidly over time but remains widely accepted in payment for current transactions. Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: It cannot be money because a perfect store of value is required.

options.label: B
options.text: It can still qualify as money because acceptance as payment is the defining criterion.

options.label: C
options.text: It can qualify as money only if it is included in bank reserves.

options.label: D
options.text: It must be excluded from money because all money must appreciate over time.

options.label: E
options.text: It can qualify as money only when its value equals the monetary base.

explanation: The course definition requires that money be accepted as a means of payment. An asset may perform the store-of-value function imperfectly and still function as money if it remains accepted for transactions.

prompt: A firm lists a machine at $50,000, a buyer keeps $50,000 in a checking account for one month, and then pays the firm. Which ordering correctly matches the functions of money?

options.label: A
options.text: Unit of account, medium of exchange, store of value

options.label: B
options.text: Store of value, unit of account, medium of exchange

options.label: C
options.text: Medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account

options.label: D
options.text: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value

options.label: E
options.text: Unit of account, store of value, medium of exchange

explanation: The listed price uses money as a unit of account, holding the balance for a month uses it as a store of value, and transferring it to the firm uses it as a medium of exchange. The ordering follows the sequence of actions.

prompt: Which condition is necessary for an asset to meet the course definition of money?

options.label: A
options.text: It must be accepted as a means of payment.

options.label: B
options.text: It must earn interest while it is held.

options.label: C
options.text: It must be part of the monetary base.

options.label: D
options.text: It must be included in M2 but excluded from M1.

options.label: E
options.text: It must be a bank deposit rather than currency.

explanation: The defining feature of money is acceptance as a means of payment. Interest earnings, deposit status, and inclusion in a particular statistical aggregate are not necessary conditions in the definition.

prompt: Initially, currency in circulation is $600 billion, reserves are $250 billion, checkable deposits are $900 billion, and savings deposits are $500 billion. Then $100 billion moves from savings to checking and reserves independently rise by $40 billion. What are the changes in M1, M2, and the monetary base?

options.label: A
options.text: M1 rises by $140 billion; M2 rises by $100 billion; MB is unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: M1 rises by $100 billion; M2 is unchanged; MB rises by $40 billion.

options.label: C
options.text: M1 rises by $100 billion; M2 rises by $100 billion; MB rises by $40 billion.

options.label: D
options.text: M1 is unchanged; M2 falls by $100 billion; MB rises by $40 billion.

options.label: E
options.text: M1 falls by $100 billion; M2 is unchanged; MB falls by $40 billion.

explanation: The savings-to-checking transfer raises M1 by $100 billion but leaves M2 unchanged. The separate $40 billion reserve increase changes only the monetary base because currency in circulation is unchanged.

prompt: The monetary base is $980 billion and M1 is $1,540 billion. Currency in circulation is $620 billion. M2 is $2,250 billion, and savings plus small time deposits total $570 billion. Which values are correct for bank reserves, checkable deposits, and retail money market mutual fund balances?

options.label: A
options.text: Reserves = $360 billion; checkable deposits = $920 billion; money market balances = $710 billion

options.label: B
options.text: Reserves = $360 billion; checkable deposits = $920 billion; money market balances = $140 billion

options.label: C
options.text: Reserves = $620 billion; checkable deposits = $560 billion; money market balances = $140 billion

options.label: D
options.text: Reserves = $920 billion; checkable deposits = $360 billion; money market balances = $140 billion

options.label: E
options.text: Reserves = $360 billion; checkable deposits = $1,540 billion; money market balances = $570 billion

explanation: Reserves are $980 - $620 = $360 billion, and checkable deposits are $1,540 - $620 = $920 billion. M2- only components total $710 billion; after subtracting $570 billion, money market balances equal $140 billion.

prompt: M1 is $1,700 billion and M2 is $2,550 billion. A $120 billion checking balance is shifted into savings, while an unrelated $50 billion of new currency enters circulation. What are the new M1 and M2?

options.label: A
options.text: M1 = $1,820 billion; M2 = $2,600 billion

options.label: B
options.text: M1 = $1,580 billion; M2 = $2,430 billion

options.label: C
options.text: M1 = $1,750 billion; M2 = $2,550 billion

options.label: D
options.text: M1 = $1,630 billion; M2 = $2,600 billion

options.label: E
options.text: M1 = $1,630 billion; M2 = $2,480 billion

explanation: The checking-to-savings shift lowers M1 by $120 billion but leaves M2 unchanged. The $50 billion currency increase raises both aggregates, so M1 changes by -$70 billion to $1,630 billion and M2 rises to $2,600 billion.

prompt: Currency in circulation is $800 billion, reserves are $300 billion, and checkable deposits are $950 billion. A person deposits $100 of currency into checking, raising reserves by $100, while another $40 of reserves is added independently. What are the new monetary base and M1?

options.label: A
options.text: Monetary base = $1,040 billion; M1 = $1,850 billion

options.label: B
options.text: Monetary base = $1,200 billion; M1 = $1,750 billion

options.label: C
options.text: Monetary base = $1,140 billion; M1 = $1,750 billion

options.label: D
options.text: Monetary base = $1,200 billion; M1 = $1,850 billion

options.label: E
options.text: Monetary base = $1,140 billion; M1 = $1,850 billion

explanation: The initial base is $1,100 billion. The deposit itself leaves the base unchanged, while the independent reserve addition raises it to $1,140 billion; the deposit also leaves M1 unchanged at $1,750 billion because currency falls as checking rises.

prompt: M2 is $3,000 billion. M1 is $2,000 billion. Savings deposits fall by $140 billion, small time deposits rise by $60 billion, retail money market mutual fund balances rise by $30 billion, and M1 rises by $20 billion. What is the new M2?

options.label: A
options.text: $2,970 billion

options.label: B
options.text: $3,110 billion

options.label: C
options.text: $2,950 billion

options.label: D
options.text: $2,890 billion

options.label: E
options.text: $3,030 billion

explanation: The change in M2 is +20 -140 +60 +30 = -30 billion. The new M2 is therefore $3,000 - $30 = $2,970 billion.

prompt: The monetary base is initially $1,300 billion. Currency in circulation rises by $90 billion, reserves fall by $140 billion, and then reserves rise independently by $25 billion. What is the new monetary base?

options.label: A
options.text: $1,415 billion

options.label: B
options.text: $1,250 billion

options.label: C
options.text: $1,275 billion

options.label: D
options.text: $1,325 billion

options.label: E
options.text: $1,185 billion

explanation: The net change in the monetary base is +90 -140 +25 = -25 billion. The new base is $1,300 - $25 = $1,275 billion.

prompt: A household moves $50 from a retail money market mutual fund balance into checking and another $30 from checking into currency. Assume no other changes in public monetary holdings. What happens to M1 and M2?

options.label: A
options.text: M1 rises by $80, while M2 rises by $50.

options.label: B
options.text: M1 rises by $30, while M2 falls by $20.

options.label: C
options.text: M1 rises by $50, while M2 is unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: M1 is unchanged, while M2 falls by $50.

options.label: E
options.text: M1 falls by $20, while M2 is unchanged.

explanation: Moving $50 from an M2-only component into checking raises M1 by $50 and leaves M2 unchanged. Moving $30 from checking to currency only reallocates funds within M1 and M2, so it does not change either total further.
